title: Flink: answers from a stream while it is still flowing
dek: Batch jobs answer yesterday's questions. Flink answers them as events arrive: clicks per ad this minute, a card used in two cities within ten minutes, the live ETA of every order. Here is how it handles time, keeps state, and recovers without counting anything twice.

items: Flink runs a graph of operators over unbounded streams, usually reading from Kafka, with state kept per key (per ad, per card, per rider).
It works in event time: windows are based on when things happened, and watermarks say when a window can be considered complete despite late arrivals.
Regular checkpoints save all state together with the source offsets, so after a failure it restores and replays: each event affects the state exactly once.

body.cap: Arrival order is an accident of the network. Counting by event time, with a watermark to decide when to stop waiting, gives the same answer every time.

items: Tumbling windows cut time into fixed blocks (clicks per minute); sliding windows overlap (the last 10 minutes, every minute); session windows close after a gap of inactivity.
A watermark is Flink's estimate that no events older than it are still coming, usually 'the newest event time seen, minus a few seconds'.
Allowed lateness keeps a window open a little longer and updates its result; events later than that go to a side output instead of disappearing.
Processing time, the clock at the moment of processing, is simpler and faster, but results change if the job is replayed.

body.label: FLINK SQL · CLICKS PER AD PER MINUTE
body.say: A Flink SQL table over the ad-clicks Kafka topic, with the click time as event time and a watermark 5 seconds behind the newest click seen. The query counts clicks per ad in one-minute tumbling windows by event time.

body.cap: Saving all operators' state and the input positions at the same logical moment is what makes a replay consistent.

items: State is partitioned by key (`keyBy(ad_id)`), so it scales with parallelism. Large state lives in RocksDB on local disk, with checkpoints in object storage.
Checkpoints run every few seconds to minutes; savepoints are manual checkpoints you take before upgrading the job, then restore from.
Exactly once applies to Flink's own state. For outputs, use sinks that commit with the checkpoint (such as Kafka's transactional sink) or writes that are idempotent.
A job can rescale from a savepoint to more or fewer parallel tasks; key groups are redistributed.
Live counts and dashboards: ad clicks, orders per area per minute, the Ad clicks problem's real-time half.
Fraud and abuse rules over sequences: the same card in two cities within 10 minutes, many failed OTPs from one device.
Features for machine learning and live ETAs: a rider's average speed over the last 5 minutes, joined with order events.
Change-data-capture pipelines that join, clean and route database changes into search, warehouses and caches. Flink SQL covers many of these without Java.

items: When numbers are needed within seconds, describe a stream job: source, key, window, state, sink.
Say event time with a watermark, and what happens to late events.
Explain recovery: checkpoints with offsets, replay, exactly-once state, idempotent or transactional output.
Keep a batch job beside it to recompute exact numbers daily, if billing depends on them.
Where it appears here: the Ad clicks problem counts clicks in minute windows with a watermark, which is this design.

body.x: Keyed state means all events for one key go to one task. If one ad gets a third of all clicks, one task does a third of the work while others idle, and the whole job slows to its pace. Pre-aggregate with a salted key (ad_id plus a random number 0 to 9), then combine the ten partial counts in a second step: the same trick as splitting a hot counter in a database.
